_doc: Ordnance tables for the field guns of the Gettysburg era from the three artillery texts: ranges by elevation, charges, projectile data, chest and battery ammunition, fuzes and small-arm cartridges. NAMES: none of these texts uses the name 'Napoleon'; the gun is the 'new 12-pdr gun' (Gibbon 1860, Appendix) or the 'light 12-pounder gun' (Instruction for Field Artillery). NOT IN THESE EDITIONS: 3-inch ordnance rifle, 10-/20-pdr Parrott, James, Whitworth, Blakely (see negative_findings, re-checked by drill_check.py). Table OCR is damaged: each table item lists OCR tokens and readings with a reading_confidence; page images were not inspected. Items marked tier 'inferred (arithmetic)' are derived by addition/multiplication from documented figures.

items.ref: Part I, Ammunition carried in each Chest (p. 19-20): light 12-pounder gun
items.paraphrase: Limber/caisson chest for the light 12-pounder gun (= the Napoleon): 12 fixed shot (184.8 lb), 12 spherical case (176.4 lb), 4 shells (48.7 lb), 4 canisters (67.6 lb) = 32 rounds, plus 2 spare cartridges of 2.5 lb, 48 friction primers, 2 yd slow-match, 4 portfires; total OCR "484-1" lb. The category labels for spherical case and friction primers are dropped by the OCR; assignment is by order and confirmed by arithmetic (sum of the legible weights 184.8+176.4+48.7+67.6+5+0.4+0.5+0.7 = 484.1).

items.ref: Part I, Ammunition carried in each Chest (p. 19): 12-pounder gun
items.paraphrase: Chest for the (heavy) 12-pounder gun: 20 shot (308 lb), 8 spherical case (117.6 lb), 4 canisters (67.6 lb) = 32 rounds, 2 spare cartridges, 48 primers, 2 yd slow-match, 4 portfires; total OCR "499 8" (= 499.8 by addition).

items.ref: Part I, Ammunition carried in each Chest (p. 19): 6-pounder gun
items.paraphrase: Chest for the 6-pounder gun: 25 shot (190 lb), 20 spherical case (140 lb), 5 canisters (42 lb) = 50 rounds, 2 spare cartridges of 1.25 lb; the OCR total reads "876-1" but the legible weights add to 376.1 lb (digit damage). 50 rounds is the PDF's "50 per rifle chest" figure, but it belongs here to the 6-pdr gun - no rifle chest is printed in any of these texts.

items.ref: Ch. XI Equipment of field carriages, "Ammunition carried in each Chest" (pp. 303-304)
items.paraphrase: The Ordnance Manual (1850 text) prints the same kind of chest table for the 6-pdr gun, 12-pdr gun, 12-pdr, 24-pdr and 32-pdr howitzers, but has NO light 12-pounder (Napoleon) chest; its column OCR is too scrambled to read counts reliably, so the Instruction for Field Artillery (1860) table is used as the primary chest source.

items.ref: School of the Piece / Manoeuvres, para 444: cannoneers seated on the chests
items.paraphrase: A caisson carries three ammunition chests: the limber chest, a middle chest and a rear chest (cannoneers sit on the limber chest and the middle chest; Nos. 6 and 7 may mount the rear chest). The same chest design fits the limber and the caisson, so a light-12 caisson holds 3 x 32 = 96 rounds (derived) and a gun with its caisson 4 x 32 = 128 rounds.
items.verbatim2: to mount the rear chest of the caisson.
items.verbatim: Nos. 3, 4, and 8 on tlic middle chest of the caisson.

items.ref: Part I Art. II, Composition and equipment of a battery for war (pp. 7-8)
items.paraphrase: War establishment table (OCR columns damaged): totals read 1,218 / 1,344 / 1,112 rounds for the three battery types; for the light-12 battery (6 guns, 12 caissons) 1,344 = 42 chests x 32 rounds, composed of 504 shot, 504 spherical case, 168 shell, 168 canister (OCR "604 504 168 168" = 504,504,168,168 by the 12:12:4:4 chest ratio). Campaign allowance is double this, about 400 rounds per piece, 200 accompanying the battery.

data.chests: six limber chests + twelve caissons x 3 = 42 chests x 32 rounds

items.reading_confidence: medium (column attribution inferred; 1,344 and 224/gun reproduce exactly from the chest table)
items.verbatim: Total number of rounds with a battery..

items.ref: Derived comparison with PDF B.6.14.2 (288/288/96/96 per six-Napoleon battery)
items.paraphrase: The PDF's "typical stock for a six-Napoleon battery: 288 solid shot, 288 spherical case, 96 shell, 96 canister" (768 rounds) equals 24 chests x (12,12,4,4): six guns each with one limber chest and one three-chest caisson (4 x 6 = 24 chests). So the PDF figure is reproduced exactly from the documented chest contents with one caisson per gun; the manual's war establishment has two caissons per gun (1,344 rounds). Both are consistent with the chest table.

items.ref: Part I Art. III, Ranges of Field Guns and Howitzers, p. 44: LIGHT 12-PDR GUN
items.paraphrase: Light 12-pounder gun (Napoleon), 2.5 lb, shot, read in pairs: 0 deg 325, 1 deg 620, 2 deg 875, 3 deg 1,200, 4 deg "1,820" (cannot exceed 5 deg; damaged digit), 5 deg 1,680 - this is the PDF's 1,680 yd (Napoleon article). Shell: 3 deg 45 min 1,300; spherical case: 3 deg 45 min 1,130 (Gibbon 1,135). So 1,619 (Gibbon appendix) and 1,680 (Instruction for Field Artillery) are both PRINTED values from the two manuals, not one value mis-copied.

No light 12-pdr appears.

items.ref: Part I Ammunition, Charges of powder (p. 11)
items.paraphrase: Service charges: 12-pdr gun and light 12-pdr gun 2.5 lb for shot (the same ammunition is used for both); 6-pdr gun 1.25 lb; 12-pdr howitzer 1.0 lb; 24-pdr howitzer 2.0 lb; 32-pdr howitzer 2.5 lb (table column OCR scrambled; confirmed by the range-table charge columns). Gibbon's range table gives the new 12-pdr 2.5 lb shot / 2.0 lb shell / 2.5 lb spherical case, matching the PDF (2.5 lb shot and case, 2.0 lb shell); the FA range-table OCR reads 2-5 for the shell, a conflict (OCR or edition) left open.
items.verbatim: The same ammunitioQ is used for the 12-pounder and light 12-poQndcr guns.

items.ref: Part I Projectiles (p. 11-12)
items.paraphrase: Canister: tin cylinder on a sabot filled with cast-iron shot in four tiers; OCR reads 21 shot for guns, 48 for howitzers. The PDF says 27 balls of 1.49 in. for the Napoleon; Gibbon's appendix canister table OCR shows "27" and diameters 1.49/1.46 for the 12-pdr class. The FA "21" is likely an OCR confusion of 27 (7->1), but this is not settled without the page image.
items.verbatim: Canisters for guns contain 21 shots each ; those for howitzers

items.ref: Part I, Charges for spherical case shot (p. 13)
items.paraphrase: Spherical case, balls per shot (OCR order 32-, 24-, 12-, 6-pdr): 245, 175, 76, 37; bursting charge 1.4/1.2/1.0/0.5 oz (OCR); loaded weight 32/24/11.77/6.55 lb. For the 12-pdr the OCR says 76 balls, 11.77 lb; the PDF says 78 balls, 12.1 lb - unresolved (76/78 digit ambiguity; weight differs).
items.verbatim: Number of musket balls Bursting charge of powder oz. Weight of shot, loaded lbs.

items.ref: Part I, Weights of fixed ammunition (p. 15)
items.paraphrase: The fixed-ammunition weight table is column-scrambled. Per-round weights (projectile + cartridge + sabot) cross-checked from the chest table: light-12/12-pdr shot round 15.4 lb, spherical-case round 14.7 lb, shell round 12.2 lb, canister round 16.9 lb; 6-pdr shot 7.6, case 7.0, canister 8.4 lb. The PDF's projectile-only weights (12.25 lb shot, 12.1 case, 12.3 shell, 14.8 canister) are not separable in this OCR; the number 14-8 does occur in the table.

items.ref: Appendix, Dimensions and Weights of Canisters
items.paraphrase: Gibbon's appendix has a canister-dimension table (large and small gauges, tiers, shot per canister); its OCR is too scrambled to read the 12-pdr gun line (27 shot in tiers is the only legible pattern: "Number of shot ... 27").

items.ref: Part I, Fuze (p. 13-14)
items.paraphrase: Bormann (Belgian) metallic time fuze: 1.5 in. disc, 0.5 in. thick, composition in a circular groove under a soft-metal cover marked in seconds and fractions up to 5.5 s; the cover is cut with the fuze-cutter/gouge to expose the composition to the discharge flame; two cutters per piece.
items.verbatim2: which is the longest time for which these fuzes are constructed.
items.verbatim: is the only kind at present used in the field artillery service.

items.ref: Ch. IX Fuzes: the paper fuze (p. ~287)
items.paraphrase: Gibbon's paper fuze: colour gives the rate - black 2, red 3, green 4, yellow 5 seconds to the inch; each fuze two inches long (yellow 10 s); shorter times by cutting with a knife; used with a conical fuze-plug pressed in by thumb. The PDF's "about 4 seconds per inch" paper fuze corresponds to the green fuze here. Gibbon also describes the Belgian "Boarmann" (Bormann) fuze as the best and most regular in use.
items.verbatim2: The Paper-Fuze, Fig. 172, is a better form, and

items.ref: Ch. IX Fuzes: Belgian (Bormann) fuze
items.paraphrase: Gibbon: the Belgian or "Boarmann" fuze is "by far the best and most regular" in use; composition pressed on end and burnt from the end, avoiding the irregularity of fuzes driven in layers; case of lead-tin composition.
items.verbatim: by far the best and most regular of anv

items.ref: Part I, Friction primers (p. 14)
items.paraphrase: Friction primer: rifle-powder tube inserted in the vent, ignited by pulling a rough wire through a friction composition (1 part potassium chlorate : 2 antimony sulphide, gum arabic); primers issued at 150 per cent of the rounds.
items.verbatim: filled with rifle powder and inserted in the vent at the moment of firing.

items.paraphrase: Ordnance Manual allowance: 200 rounds to each piece, in the reserves and in the active batteries; what the caissons cannot carry is kept in boxes with the reserves.
items.verbatim: 200 rounds to each piece, both of the reserves and of the active batteries.
